newsitem.title: BELARUS: Police, protesters clash as Belarus tension rises.
newsitem.headline: Police, protesters clash as Belarus tension rises.

text.p: Belarus police and demonstrators clashed on Sunday in central Minsk amid mounting tension over President Alexander Lukashenko's bid to boost his powers and stifle opposition in the former Soviet republic.
Police wielding riot shields beat protesters with truncheons and arrested more than 10. Some 20 people were injured, organisers of the demonstration told Reuters.
The demonstrators carried white and red Belarussian tricolour flags during their "March of Silence" towards the parliament building, focus of opposition to Lukashenko's plans.

They dispersed after several hours and deputies urged the protesters to return at 2 p.m. (1200 GMT) on Monday, when parliament is due to hold an emergency session on the political situation in Belarus.
Opposition deputies have said they will start impeachment proceedings against the president, although it is not clear if this will be on the agenda at Monday's session.
"I was beaten with a truncheon," Stanislav Bogdankevich, leader of the United Civic party and parliamentary opposition, told a news conference.
"They taught me a lesson for agreeing with Lukashenko," he said ironically, referring to his former central bank post.

The demonstrators say Lukashenko is seeking dictatorial powers. He says his presidency is a crusade against corruption in the country of 10 million and he has vowed to dismiss anybody who does not recognise the vote.

In a statement issued late on Sunday Lukashenko's Security Council said there had been no violence during the protests, which it said had been organised by "national extremists" bent on destabilising the country.

It also slammed foreign media, especially Russia's NTV commercial television, for their coverage of the demonstration, saying they deliberately exaggerated what had happened. It threatened to ban NTV broadcasts from Belarussian territory.

The march, attended by between 5,000 and 10,000 people, was the latest in a series of protests against Lukashenko's proposals, which would allow him to extend his term in office by two years without new elections.
"Long live Belarus," the marchers chanted, grumbling about Lukashenko's efforts to create a union with neighbouring Russia.

Some marchers wore cloth gags to symbolise the way the Belarussian media has covered previous protest actions of this kind. Local radio made no mention of the march, but continued its relentless drive to encourage people to turn out and vote.
The referendum officially takes place next Sunday, but polling stations are already open.
Lukashenko sent all voters a colour postcard of himself on Saturday and urged them to vote.
"Mafia clans and the owners of ill-gotten capital have united against the president you elected," he wrote on the card, which showed him standing hand on heart before an adoring crowd.
"I turn to you, the honest people, to help save the country for the sake of our common future."
His supporters said people should vote before November 24, when questions drafted by parliament will also be on the ballot paper.
Some deputies have been staying in parliament around the clock because they fear the president will close the building, which has been picketted by opposition demonstrators.
